hotel-ev-charging-guest-convenience-reve.title: 酒店要不要装充电桩？先看住客停车多久、车位够不够
hotel-ev-charging-guest-convenience-reve.titleEn: Should a Hotel Install EV Chargers? Start with Guests’ Parking Time and Available Spaces
hotel-ev-charging-guest-convenience-reve.description: 酒店充电设施应先方便住客，再核对经营贡献。从停车时长、车位供需、住宿与餐饮增量和实际成本，判断建设规模与收费方式。
hotel-ev-charging-guest-convenience-reve.descriptionEn: Start with guest convenience, then verify the business contribution. Assess parking duration, available spaces, incremental rooms and food and beverage business, and actual costs before choosing the scale and pricing of hotel EV charging.
hotel-ev-charging-guest-convenience-reve.author: 迈创兄弟C&T（MarvelBros C&T）
content: 客人开着新能源汽车来到酒店，希望停车、休息之后，第二天能顺利继续出发。对酒店来说，充电服务首先应该解决这件事。客人用得方便，酒店才有机会把这项设施变成选店理由、消费机会和持续收益。
因此，要不要装充电桩，不能只从设备价格开始讨论。更有用的起点是：哪些客人需要充电，他们的车停多久，酒店能否提供方便可靠的服务，以及这项服务能给经营带来什么贡献。停车时长与车位数量，都是回答这些问题的依据。
国家能源局10月8日公布，2026年国庆假期前三天，纳入监测的全国高速公路新能源汽车充电次数同比增长48.41%。这一数据说明长途出行中的补电需求正在增长，统计对象却不是酒店住客。酒店仍需回到自己的客群，判断需求会不会在本店出现。
让充电成为客人容易使用的服务
充电服务的价值，在客人抵店前就可能开始发挥作用。Marriott Bonvoy的公路旅行搜索说明显示，客人可以按电动汽车充电设施筛选沿途酒店。这至少说明，对于有补电需要的旅客，充电设施可以成为选店条件。
酒店要把这项便利说清楚：设备是否可用，适配条件是什么，住客能否预约或优先使用，充电与停车怎样收费。若无法保证抵店时有空位，就应说明使用方式和附近替代地点，避免把“提供充电设施”理解成“任何时候都能立即充电”。
抵店后，客人应能找到车位、看懂操作和费用，有问题时知道找谁。酒店不必给充电服务增加很多额外环节，但需要让前台掌握准确的信息。如果客人为了启动充电反复下载软件、确认身份，或在停车场与前台之间来回询问，设备虽然已经安装，便利却没有完整交付。
停多久，决定客人需要怎样的充电安排
过夜住客与短停客人的时间条件不同。住一晚的客人可能愿意在休息时补电；参加会议或来餐厅用餐的客人，可能只有一个较短的停留窗口。酒店应先弄清这些时间，再讨论充电功率与设备数量。
美国能源部的公共充电指南将酒店列为适合结合较长停车时间规划充电的场所。这一原则值得借鉴，但不能据此认定所有酒店都适合同一种设备。车辆当前电量、需要补充的电量、车型及场地条件，都影响具体方案。
先观察本店工作日与周末的抵离店规律，了解客人希望在离开前达到什么补电程度。若主要需求发生在夜间，服务重点可能是停车后容易开始充电、使用过程稳定，以及合理的占位安排。若短停需求多，就要比较有限时间内能够提供的补电服务与客人的实际期望。
车位是否够用，也不能只看酒店总共有多少停车位。充电位在同一时段有多少需求，普通住客停车是否紧张，充满后能否安全合理地释放车位，都关系到体验。夜间频繁要求熟睡的住客下楼挪车，可能降低这项服务的便利；一辆车长期占位，也可能让其他客人无法使用。规则要结合本店停车条件制定，并在客人使用前说明。
酒店可以从哪里获得收益
充电的直接收入比较容易识别：酒店自营时可能收取充电服务费用，与运营商合作时可能获得约定分成或场地收入。具体收入属于谁、电费与维修费由谁承担、结算怎样核对，都应按实际合作安排确认。
住宿业务的机会在于，充电便利能否帮助酒店获得原本可能选择其他物业的订单，或满足现有客户的新需求。市场销售团队可以从住客咨询、协议客户要求和预订反馈中寻找证据。已经订房的客人使用了充电桩，并不意味着这笔房费都是充电设施带来的增量。
餐饮与休闲业务也可能受益。例如，有补电需求的客人在酒店用餐期间充电，充电便利便可能支持这次消费。但酒店需要确认，消费是因便利而新增，还是客人本来就会发生的支出。不能把充电时段内所有餐厅营业额都归到充电项目名下。
ChargePoint发布的Oxford Collection案例介绍了该酒店集团如何将充电与过夜住宿、会议活动和企业客户需要结合，并通过系统掌握使用与等待情况。这是供给方公布的实践线索，可以帮助酒店理解服务场景；案例没有提供可供照搬的独立利润增量证明。
方便与收费，可以同时成立
充电服务不必一律免费。客人购买的是清楚、可靠、适合行程的便利，收费方式应与酒店定位、客群需要和实际成本相配。
对住宿客人，酒店可以比较单独收费、明确额度的住宿权益，以及运营商直接收费等安排。若把充电包含在房价或套餐内，要说明额度、使用条件和超出部分的费用，财务也要核算酒店承担的成本，不能把“包含”当成没有成本。
对餐饮或会议客人，可以根据停车时长与消费场景研究相应安排。优惠是否值得提供，要看新增业务贡献，而非使用人数是否热闹。充电服务费、停车费及可能的超时费用，应在使用前清楚呈现；让客人离店时才发现额外收费，会削弱便利设施原本希望建立的信任。
对社会车辆开放，可能扩大使用量，也可能挤占住客车位。停车紧张的酒店，必须先保证核心住宿服务。如果外部充电收入增加，却使住客难以停车或充电，项目的整体经营结果未必更好。
用一张表，把便利与收益放在一起核对
总经理可以组织前厅、市场销售、工程与财务建立一张“充电服务便利与收益核对表”。无需先追求复杂系统，关键是让服务结果与经营结果能够相互对照。
服务端记录使用客群、停车时段、充电需求、是否成功使用、等待与故障情况，以及客人反馈。把“设备运行时间”与“客人需要时能够使用”区分开，才能识别真正影响便利的时段。
经营端分别记录充电收入或合作分成、相关住宿与餐饮业务证据，以及电费、平台费用、维护和新增人工。再核对车位是否因此影响其他业务。成本已由酒店承担还是已被运营商分成扣除，要先核清，避免重复扣减或漏算。
这张表还应区分两种判断：某段时间的运行贡献是否为正，以及长期投资是否值得。前者不自动证明后者。设备、施工及可能的供电改造投入，需要在长期测算中体现，不能因为当月充电收入超过电费，就宣布项目已经盈利或能够回本。
住宿和餐饮的增量难以直接归因时，可以先记录客人明确提到的选店原因、充电咨询后的预订结果，以及相近经营条件下的变化。价格、促销、活动和季节都会影响结果；一个短期观察可以支持继续研究，不能独自证明充电设施造成了增长。
安装与维护，为便利和收益提供保障
在决定建设规模前，酒店仍需确认停车场使用权、当地适用要求、供电条件和施工安排，并由合格专业人员评估方案。设备选择应与服务目标匹配，不能只比较功率大小或采购报价。
合作运营时，要明确设备故障谁响应、信息由谁更新、费用怎样结算，以及服务停止时如何处理住客安排。维修与交付的意义，是让酒店承诺的便利持续可用，而不只是完成一次安装。
已有试行条件的酒店，可以先选择能够代表主要客群的范围，持续记录服务与经营情况；尚不具备条件的酒店，可以先完善附近充电信息与出行协助，同时补齐需求和场地资料。存在电力或安全问题时应停止使用并交专业人员处理；若长期需求不足、收益无法覆盖投入，或住客停车体验持续受损，就应调整规模、规则或合作方式。
下一次经营会，可以先让团队回答一个具体问题：客人在本店停留的这段时间，充电服务能为他省去什么麻烦，又能为酒店留下什么经过核对的贡献？把这个问题回答清楚，设备数量和经营模式才有了选择依据。

contentEn: Guests arriving at a hotel in an electric vehicle want to park, rest and continue their journey smoothly the next day. A hotel's charging service should first meet that need. When the service is convenient to use, the hotel has an opportunity to make it a reason to book, a source of additional spending and a contributor to recurring income.

The decision to install EV chargers should therefore begin with more than equipment prices. A more useful starting point is to ask which guests need charging, how long their vehicles remain parked, whether the hotel can provide a convenient and reliable service, and what contribution that service can make to the business. Parking duration and the number of available spaces help answer these questions.

On October 8, China's National Energy Administration reported that, during the first three days of the 2026 National Day holiday, the number of charging sessions for new energy vehicles at monitored expressway locations nationwide increased by 48.41% year on year. This indicates growing demand for recharging during long-distance journeys, but the figures do not describe hotel guests. Each hotel still needs to assess its own guest segments to determine whether that demand will arise at the property.
Make charging easy for guests to use

Charging can offer value before a guest arrives. Marriott Bonvoy's guidance on searching for hotels along a road trip route shows that travelers can filter properties by electric vehicle charging facilities. At a minimum, this demonstrates that charging facilities can be a hotel selection criterion for travelers who need to recharge.

Hotels should explain the service clearly: whether the equipment is available, its compatibility requirements, whether in-house guests can reserve a space or receive priority, and how charging and parking are priced. If a vacant charging space cannot be guaranteed on arrival, explain how the service works and identify nearby alternatives. “Charging facilities available” should not be understood to mean “immediate charging available at any time.”

Once at the property, guests should be able to find the space, understand the operating instructions and charges, and know whom to contact if something goes wrong. Hotels do not need to add numerous steps to the service, but the front desk needs accurate information. If guests repeatedly have to download apps, verify their identity or walk between the car park and the front desk just to start charging, the equipment may be installed, but the promised convenience has not been fully delivered.
Parking duration determines the charging arrangement guests need

Overnight guests and short-stay visitors have different time constraints. A guest staying overnight may be willing to recharge while resting; a meeting attendee or restaurant patron may have only a shorter window. Hotels should understand those timeframes before discussing charging power and the number of chargers.

The U.S. Department of Energy's public charging guidance identifies hotels as locations where charging can be planned around longer parking durations. This principle is useful, but it does not establish that every hotel needs the same equipment. A vehicle's current charge, the amount of energy needed, the vehicle model and site conditions all affect the appropriate solution.

Start by observing weekday and weekend arrival and departure patterns, and understand how much charge guests want before leaving. If demand is mainly overnight, service priorities may include an easy start after parking, reliable operation and sensible arrangements for occupying charging spaces. If short-duration demand is more common, compare the charging service that can be delivered within the available time with guests' actual expectations.

Parking capacity cannot be assessed from the property's total number of spaces alone. Demand for charging spaces at the same time, pressure on ordinary guest parking and whether a space can be released safely and reasonably after charging all affect the experience. Frequently asking sleeping guests to come downstairs and move their vehicles at night may reduce convenience; a vehicle occupying a space for too long may prevent other guests from charging. Rules should reflect the property's parking conditions and be explained before use.
Where can the hotel earn income?

Direct charging income is relatively easy to identify. A hotel operating the service itself may charge a service fee; one working with a charging operator may receive an agreed revenue share or income for use of the site. The actual agreement should establish who receives the income, who pays for electricity and repairs, and how settlement figures are reconciled.

For the rooms business, the opportunity is whether charging convenience helps the hotel win bookings that might otherwise go to another property, or meets new needs among existing clients. The sales and marketing team can look for evidence in guest enquiries, negotiated account requirements and booking feedback. An already-booked guest's use of a charger does not mean that all room revenue from the stay is incremental revenue generated by the charging facility.

Food and beverage and leisure outlets may also benefit. For example, a guest who needs to recharge may do so while dining at the hotel, and that convenience may support the visit. The hotel still needs to establish whether the spending is additional because of that convenience or would have occurred anyway. All restaurant revenue earned during charging hours cannot be attributed to the charging project.

ChargePoint's Oxford Collection case study describes how the hotel group connects charging with overnight stays, meetings and events, and corporate client needs, while using its system to understand usage and waiting. This supplier-published account offers practical insight into service scenarios. It does not provide independently verified evidence of incremental profit that other hotels can simply adopt.
Convenience and charging fees can coexist

Charging does not have to be free in every case. Guests are paying for a clear, reliable convenience that fits their itinerary. Pricing should reflect the hotel's positioning, guest needs and actual costs.

For overnight guests, a hotel can compare separate charging fees, a stay benefit with a clearly defined allowance, and direct payment to the charging operator. If charging is included in the room rate or a package, specify the allowance, conditions of use and charges beyond the allowance. Finance should also account for the costs borne by the hotel: “included” does not mean cost-free.

For restaurant patrons or meeting attendees, arrangements can be considered in relation to parking duration and the purpose of the visit. Whether a discount is worthwhile depends on its contribution to additional business, rather than the apparent popularity of the service. Charging service fees, parking fees and any overstay charges should be clearly presented before use. Discovering extra charges only at departure can undermine the trust that the amenity was intended to build.

Opening charging to the public may increase usage, but it may also take parking spaces away from in-house guests. Hotels with limited parking must first protect their core accommodation service. If public charging income rises while guests struggle to park or charge, the overall business outcome may not improve.
Review convenience and contribution on one worksheet

The general manager can bring together front office, sales and marketing, engineering and finance to create a charging service convenience and contribution worksheet. A complex system is not the first requirement. The key is to assess service outcomes alongside business outcomes.

On the service side, record user segments, parking periods, charging needs, successful use, waiting and faults, and guest feedback. Distinguishing equipment uptime from availability when guests actually need the service helps identify the periods that matter to convenience.

On the business side, separately record charging income or revenue share, evidence relating to rooms and food and beverage business, and electricity costs, platform fees, maintenance and additional labor. Then assess whether the use of parking spaces affects other business. Establish whether a cost is borne directly by the hotel or has already been deducted from the operator's revenue share, to avoid double counting or omissions.

The worksheet should also distinguish two questions: whether the operating contribution is positive over a given period, and whether the long-term investment is worthwhile. The first does not automatically prove the second. Equipment, installation and any required electrical infrastructure upgrades belong in the long-term assessment. Charging income exceeding electricity costs in one month is not sufficient to declare that the project is profitable or will achieve payback.

When incremental rooms or food and beverage business is difficult to attribute directly, begin by recording guests' stated reasons for choosing the hotel, bookings following charging enquiries, and changes under comparable operating conditions. Rates, promotions, events and seasonality all affect results. A short observation period can support further investigation, but cannot by itself prove that charging facilities caused growth.
Installation and maintenance support convenience and contribution

Before deciding the scale of the installation, the hotel still needs to confirm its rights to use the car park, applicable local requirements, electrical capacity and construction arrangements, and have qualified professionals assess the proposal. Equipment should match the service objectives; charging power and purchase price alone are insufficient grounds for selection.

Where an operator is involved, clarify who responds to equipment faults, who updates service information, how charges are settled and how guest arrangements will be handled if the service stops. Maintenance and handover matter because they keep the hotel's promised convenience available over time, rather than merely completing an installation.

Hotels able to run a pilot can start within a scope representative of their main guest segments and continue to record service and business performance. Properties not yet ready can improve information about nearby charging and provide travel assistance while gathering the demand and site information they need. Electrical or safety problems require suspension of use and attention from qualified professionals. If long-term demand is insufficient, returns cannot cover the investment, or guest parking continues to suffer, the hotel should adjust the scale, rules or operating arrangement.

At the next operations meeting, start with one specific question: during the time a guest spends at this property, what inconvenience can charging remove, and what verified contribution can it leave for the hotel? Once the team can answer that clearly, it has a basis for choosing the number of chargers and the operating model.
